title: Strength-toughness enhancement in sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar ferrite-martensite dual-phase steel at −84 °C extreme low-temperature conditions
abstract: This study proposes a novel quenching- intercritical quenching (Q-IQ) process to fabricate a ferrite-martensite dual-phase steel with sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar (HL) structures. The final HL microstructure exhibited a uniform lamellar distribution of ferrite (45.3 %, average width 0.39 μm) and martensite (54.7 %, average width 0.37 μm), along with a relatively high fraction of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs, 42.8 %). Mechanical testing at –84 °C demonstrates superior performance, with an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 1007 MPa, total elongation (El) of 24 %, and impact energy (Akv) of 187 J. Microstructural analysis indicates that the sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar architecture structure promotes a more uniform stress distribution and promotes cooperative deformation between soft and hard phases. The nucleation of voids is not limited to the hard martensitic phase, and the interfaces remain intact, which significantly improves the cooperative deformation between the soft and hard phases. Sustained work hardening at –84 °C was enabled by cooperative deformation and heterogeneous deformation-induced (HDI) hardening. Additionally, the sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar structure promotes a high-volume fraction of HAGBs and facilitates the uniform distribution of both HAGBs and voids, thereby enhancing the impact toughness at –84 °C.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: With the accelerated melting of Arctic glaciers due to global warming, Arctic shipping routes are gaining increasing strategic and commercial significance [ 1–4 ]. However, hull structural steels suffer significant reductions in ductility and toughness at subzero temperatures [ 5–7 ]. In particular, at –84 °C conditions typical of polar waters, ships constructed from conventional high-strength steels are highly susceptible to catastrophic failure upon collision with common Arctic obstacles such as drifting ice. Such incidents pose substantial risks to cargo vessels made from conventional metallic materials, potentially leading to severe casualties and major property losses. Consequently, the development and optimization of high-strength steels with adequate plasticity and low-temperature toughness at –84 °C are essential to ensure the structural reliability and safety of ships operating in Arctic environments [ 8–12 ].

However, a trade-off between strength and low-temperature toughness remains a critical challenge under extreme low-temperature conditions [ 13–16 ]. Consequently, significant research has been dedicated to enhancing low-temperature toughness without sacrificing strength [ 17–19 ]. Heterostructured steels have increasingly attracted attention as a promising solution to balance strength and low-temperature toughness [ 20–22 ]. Liu et al. [ 23 ] developed a Fe-Cr-Ni-Co-Mo maraging steel with core–shell austenite, enabling stepwise martensitic transformation to enhance cryogenic toughness. Assisted by Laves phase strengthening, the alloy achieved >1200 MPa yield strength (YS) and >90 J toughness at −196.15°C, showing that austenite chemical heterogeneity can effectively balance strength and low-temperature toughness. Similarly, Kim et al. [ 24 ] focused on enhancing the cryogenic toughness of 9 wt% Ni steel through a quenching-lamellarizing-tempering (QLT) treatment. This process yielded a high retained austenite fraction and tailored micro-hardness distribution, achieving Charpy toughness of 238 J at –196 °C and 217 J at –253 °C. The unique soft–hard phase architecture created by QLT deflected cracks and absorbed energy, underscoring effectiveness of heterostructured steels in sub –196 °C applications. In another study, Romero-Resendiz et al. [ 25 ] explored the cryogenic performance of a heterostructured and antimicrobial 316L + Cu stainless steel (HS&AMSS), demonstrating 1400 MPa YS and 36 % ductility at −196.15°C. In-situ neutron diffraction revealed real-time phase evolution during deformation, with the exceptional performance attributed to synergistic strengthening and hardening mechanisms, highlighting HS&AMSS as a strong candidate for cryogenic applications. However, the study by Romero-Resendiz did not verify the influence of this processing route on impact toughness under low-temperature conditions. Shang et al. [ 26 ] developed a low-density steel with enhanced low-temperature toughness via hot rolling, intercritical quenching, and tempering, achieving Charpy impact energy of 61 J at –40 °C. The improvement was attributed to laminar ferrite–martensite heterostructures, which promoted secondary cracking and increased crack propagation energy due to anisotropic grain boundary distributions and a strong {001}〈110〉 texture. Although these advancements have significantly improved the low-temperature performance of high-strength steels, the challenge of simultaneously achieving superior cryogenic toughness and high strength remains insufficiently resolved, presenting an ongoing barrier to their practical use in extreme low-temperature environments.

To further improve the balance between strength and cryogenic toughness, recent studies have focused on ferrite–martensite dual-phase heterostructured steels, aiming to optimize performance through microstructural tailoring. Ferrite–martensite dual-phase steels, as first-generation high-strength steels, are widely used due to their low cost, simple processing, and favorable properties compared to single-phase steels [ 27–29 ]. In dual-phase steels, the mechanical properties reported for dual-phase steels vary widely, primarily due to differences in the volume fraction and morphology of ferrite and martensite phases [ 30–33 ]. Dual-phase steels are classified as blocky, mixed, or lamellar based on phase morphology, with extensive research focusing on the relationship between structure and mechanical performance. However, stress concentrations at the interfaces between constituent phases due to microstructural heterogeneity significantly degrade the ductility and toughness of dual-phase steels under service conditions. For instance, Ebrahimian et al. [ 34 ] studied the effect of carbon and other alloy element distribution on the hardening behavior of ferrite in ferrite-martensite dual-phase steels. Wang et al. [ 35 ] analyzed the impact fracture behavior of lamellar martensite and blocky ferrite at low temperatures, suggesting that fracture preferentially occurs in the blocky ferrite phase. Niu et al. [ 27 ] developed a micrometer-scale lamellar ferrite-martensite dual-phase steel through multiple quenching cycles. Compared to the bulk structure, it exhibits enhanced strength and ductility, which is attributed to the coordinated effect between the heterogeneous lamellar structure and strain-induced heterogeneous hardening. However, the distinct features of heterogeneous structures significantly influence the deformation behavior of dual-phase steels under tensile loading. In conventional bulk structures, excessive stress concentration at the interfaces can lead to premature void formation, resulting in early failure of the material [ 36 ]. To address this issue, researchers have developed dual-phase steels with micrometer-scale heterogeneous lamellar structures, in which void formation is preferentially observed in the hard phase [ 37 ]. This indicates that when the lamellar structure reaches the micrometer scale, a synergistic deformation effect can mitigate interface stress concentrations. However, stress concentration localized within the hard phase continues to hinder further enhancements in the tensile properties of dual-phase steels. Therefore, further refining and homogenizing the heterogeneous microstructure in ferrite-martensite dual-phase steels offers a promising strategy to overcome above limitations and achieve performance breakthroughs.

In this study, we prepare a ferrite-martensite dual-phase steel with sub-micron-scale heterogeneous lamellar microstructure using the quenching-intercritical quenching method. We systematically examine the effect of further refining the sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar structure on the steel's mechanical properties at –84 °C. Specifically, through precise control of the microstructure, we achieve a sub-micron-scale ferrite-martensite heterogeneous lamellar structure in the dual-phase steel, which exhibits excellent mechanical properties at –84 °C (ultimate tensile strength, UTS: 1007 MPa, total elongation, El: 24 %, impact energy, Akv: 161 J). The sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar structure is the key to achieving these outstanding properties. This study provides new insights and references for enhancing the safety and performance of hull structural steels in –84 °C environments, with significant scientific and engineering implications.

sections.heading: Processing route
paragraphs:
The nominal chemical composition of the two experimental steels used in this study is Fe-0.06C-0.08Si-1.15Mn-0.52Cr-4.65Ni-0.52Mo-0.035Nb (wt.%). The steels were produced in a 90-ton electric arc furnace at Wuyang Iron & Steel Co., Ltd., Henan, with a final plate length of 6000 mm, width of 4000 mm, and thickness of 45 mm. The steels underwent several pretreatment steps, including arc melting, vacuum carbon deoxidation, ladle furnace refining, wire feeding, secondary vacuum degassing treatment, mold casting, electrode preparation, electroslag remelting, slow cooling, ingot transfer, surface cleaning, (heated) bloom forging, hydrogen diffusion treatment, and (heated) rolling into 45 mm-thick plates. Dividing the rolling process into two stages not only refines the grains but also helps prevent cracking caused by excessive deformation during rolling[ 38 ]. For the heterogeneous lamellar steel (HL), the heat treatment involved quenching at 880 ± 25 °C, intercritical quenching at 680 ℃, and tempering at 540 ± 25 ℃, resulting in a sub-micron ferrite–martensite dual-phase structure. In contrast, the martensitic steel (MS) was obtained by quenching at 880 ± 25 °C followed by tempering at 540 ± 25 ℃. The rolling process is shown in  Fig. 1a 
                         , the heat treatment process for HL and MS are shown in  Fig. 1b and c , respectively.

sections.heading: Mechanical performance testing
paragraphs: Tensile tests at –84 °C were conducted in accordance with GB/T 228.3–2019 using a microcomputer-controlled electronic universal testing machine (WANCE, ETM 504C). The loading–unloading-reloading (LUR) tensile test consisted of repeated loading and unloading cycles. The loading stage was conducted at a strain rate of 10 -4  /s, and unloading was performed every 1 % strain at a rate of 1 N/s until the load dropped to 100 N. This cycle was repeated until a decrease in stress was observed. The specimen had a gauge length of 25 mm and a diameter of 5 mm. The tensile rate was 0.375 mm/min before yielding and 3.6 mm/min after yielding. Charpy impact tests at –84 °C were performed according to GB/T 19748–2019 using a pendulum impact testing machine (INSTRON, MPX). The specimen dimensions were 55 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm, with a V-notch depth of 2 mm.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs: The microstructure was observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Zeiss Gemini 350, the accelerating voltage was 15 kV), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS, Oxford Ultim MAX, the accelerating voltage was 15 kV) was employed to analyze the elemental differences in different regions. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford Instruments C-Swift + ) was performed at 20 kV with a step size of 110 nm; data were processed using AZtecCrystal software. EBSD specimens were ground and polished, then manually polished for 5 h using a colloidal silica suspension (0.02 μm). TEM specimens were mechanically thinned to 30 μm, punched into 3 mm discs, and then twin-jet electropolished at –20 °C in a solution of 8 % perchloric acid in ethanol under 25 V using a TJ-100BE electropolisher. Final thinning of the discs was performed using a TJ-100BE twin-jet electropolisher at –20 °C in an 8 % perchloric acid–ethanol solution under an applied voltage of 25 V. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using a Rigaku SmartLab 9 kW diffractometer equipped with a Cu Kα radiation source, operating at 45 kV and 200 mA, with a scanning rate of 1°/min. Quantitative evaluation of phase size and volume fraction was performed using Image-Pro Plus software.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The engineering stress–strain curves for MS and HL are shown in  Fig. 2a 
                         , with the table in the figure presenting partial results of the tensile tests at –84 °C. The impact results at –84 °C are shown in  Fig. 2e . Both MS and HL exhibit UTS exceeding 1000 MPa, demonstrating high strength. The YS of HL(MS) is 905 MPa(1054 MPa). Notably, despite similar UTS values, HL exhibits El of 24 % and Akv of 187 J, significantly outperforming MS, which shows only 16 % and 161 J, respectively. These results demonstrate that the design of the ferrite-martensite lamellar dual-phase structure effectively enhances both ductility and low-temperature toughness at –84 °C.

During the fracture process, stress concentration at the crack tip induces the transformation of residual austenite into martensite, consuming energy and thereby suppressing void and microcrack nucleation and growth, which enhances fracture toughness [ 39 , 40 ]. The transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect typically occurs in the steady stage after the rapid decline of the work hardening rate[ 41 ]. To assess the contribution of the TRIP effect, XRD measurements were performed to quantify the volume fraction of residual austenite in MS and HL.  Fig. 2c  presents the XRD patterns of both steels, indicating the absence of FCC diffraction peaks. Therefore, the influence of TRIP on the improvement of ductility and toughness can be excluded. The work hardening behavior of the two steels was analyzed using the Kocks-Mecking method.  Fig. 2b  illustrates the variation in work hardening rate with true stress for MS and HL, both exhibiting similar trends. The work hardening rate is calculated using the following formula [ 42 , 43 ]:

                         where  θ  is the work hardening rate,  σ  is the stress and  ε  is the strain. Both steels undergo three stages: rapid decline, steady, and subsequent decline. Throughout most of the strain range, HL exhibits a higher work hardening rate than MS. During the initial stage, dislocation slip in ferrite provides additional hardening, leading to a distinct hardening behavior in this stage [ 44 ]. In the second stage, the hard phase in the dual-phase steel contributes effectively to work hardening. In previous studies, interface damage occurred due to the inability of the soft and hard phases to coordinate deformation effectively, resulting in the work hardening capacity being unable to be maintained over a wide range of strains [ 27 ]. However, in the HL involved in this study, the soft and hard phases maintain good coordination during deformation, preventing interface damage and stress concentration. Therefore, after MS loses its work hardening effect (strain range: 6.6 % to 14.3 %), HL still retains its work hardening capacity.

Fig. 2d  shows the experimental load–deflection curves of MS and HL at –84 °C, with the inset presenting the full profile of the load–deflection curve. The inset highlights the five stages the material undergoes during impact, namely: I − elastic deformation, II − plastic deformation, III − ductile propagation, IV − brittle propagation, and V − ductile fracture. The characteristic points of the curve are denoted as the general yield load (P GY ), the maximum load (P M ), the fast fracture load (PF), and the fracture arrest load (PA)[ 45–48 ]. For MS steel, the maximum load corresponds to a deflection of 2.0 mm, and the PF is slightly lower than the maximum load. In addition, fast crack propagation occurs directly in the core of the impact specimen, with a corresponding deflection below 7 mm, indicating a very high crack propagation rate. After the introduction of critical tempering (HL steel), a new type of load–deflection curve is observed. Critical tempering reduces both PM and PGY by approximately 20 % and significantly prolongs the stable crack propagation stage. Compared with MS steel, the PF of HL steel decreases by about 50 %. Crack propagation during the fast fracture stage in HL steel is characterized by relatively high absorbed energy compared with MS steel, leading to an impact energy of 187 J. Regarding the fracture arrest load (PA), HL steel exhibits a value significantly higher than that of MS steel.

Based on this correspondence between fracture surface regions and the stages in the load–deflection curve, we can further analyze the differences in energy absorption and crack propagation behavior between HL and MS steels. As shown in  Fig. 2e , the fracture initiation energy of HL is slightly lower than that of MS (39 J vs 42 J); however, notable differences emerge between the two steels after reaching the peak impact load. In MS, the impact load rapidly decreases after reaching the peak, with the region corresponding to stage IV of the full profile load–deflection curve transitioning into a nearly vertical sharp drop. In contrast, stage IV in HL exhibits a progressively smoother trend. The crack propagation energies for HL and MS are 148 J and 119 J, respectively. The area under stage IV of the actual load–deflection curve is substantially larger for HL than for MS. This indicates that the sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar dual-phase structure achieves enhanced low-temperature toughness by absorbing more energy during unstable crack propagation.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs:
To elucidate the underlying mechanism for the superior mechanical properties of HL steel compared to MS steel, microstructural analyses were conducted on the samples before tensile and impact testing.  Fig. 3a and b 
                          present the SEM images of MS and HL, respectively. MS exhibits a traditional martensitic structure, characterized by fine, needle-like structures, with the lamellae arranged roughly parallel to each other. In contrast, HL exhibits a heterogeneous lamellar structure composed of alternating sub-micron ferrite and martensite. Compared to MS, the martensite lamellae in HL are much narrower. For indexation, we used the body-centered cubic (BCC) structure of α-Fe, which is representative of the ferritic phase and martensitic phase in ferrite-martensite dual-phase steel steel. The crystallographic data for α-Fe were obtained from the internal database of the EBSD software(Oxford Instruments Aztec). The grain boundary contrast (BC) along with the distribution map of grain boundaries (GB) in HL steel, as well as the distribution maps of ferrite (F, 45.3 %) and martensite (M, 54.7 %) classified using AZtecCrystal software, are shown in  Fig. 3c and d , respectively. In  Fig. 3c , it can be observed that the contrast of ferrite (green) is effectively lower than that of martensite (blue), which appears white. This confirms the distinct structural characteristics of the two steels: the microstructure of MS steel is primarily composed of tempered martensite, whereas HL exhibits a lamellar structure with alternating 45.3 % ferrite and 54.7 % martensite. Notably, the sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar ferrite-martensite dual-phase steel was successfully fabricated through tailored microstructural control.

The Kernel Average Misorientation (KAM) maps for HL and MS are shown in  Fig. 3e . The stress distribution in HL is more uniform, whereas in MS, it forms an uneven block-like distribution (as indicated by the red dashed line in  Fig. 3e ). In both HL and MS, the martensitic phase is the region where stress concentrations occur. In HL, however, due to the sub-micron ferritic phase's segregation of the martensitic phase, large block-like stress concentration regions, as seen in MS, do not form. Instead, the stress concentration is uniformly distributed, significantly alleviating the concentration of stresses. The average KAM value of HL (0.63°) is lower than that of MS (0.68°). It should be noted that the KAM value of the HL sample subjected to quenching followed by intercritical quenching is lower than that of the MS sample subjected only to quenching before tempering (0.70° vs. 0.73°), thereby excluding the influence of the final tempering. This indicates that the introduction of lamellar ferrite in HL effectively reduces the overall dislocation density compared to conventional single-phase martensitic steel (MS). This reduction in dislocation density contributes to higher plastic elongation ( Fig. 2 ) [ 49 , 50 ]. Therefore, compared to MS, HL exhibits higher elongation.

Low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs, misorientation angles ranging from 2° to 15°) and high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs, misorientation angles exceeding 15°) in the sample were analyzed by EBSD. Martensite blocks are typically separated by HAGBs, with misorientation angles ranging from 50° to 60° according to the Kurdjumov-Sachs (K-S) orientation relationship [ 51 ]. Therefore, EBSD orientation maps are employed to analyze the block structure in martensite.  Fig. 4a and b  show the inverse pole figure (IPF) of HL and MS, respectively, while  Fig. 4c and e 
                          present the misorientation distributions for HL and MS. The misorientation across martensitic block boundaries in HL and MS steels was measured using the line-intercept method, as shown in  Fig. 4d and f . Martensitic block boundaries were defined as HAGBs with misorientation angles greater than 50°, and the spacing between such boundaries was designated as D block  (the specific block size will be discussed in 4.2 section). Compared to MS, intercritical quenching resulted in an increase in the fraction of boundaries with misorientation angles exceeding 50° in HL, rising from 35.2 % to 42.8 %.

To further elucidate the superior plasticity and low-temperature toughness of HL at –84 °C, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was employed to examine the fracture microstructure before and after the Charpy impact test. The TEM bright-field image of HL is shown in  Fig. 5a 
                         . Similar to the SEM and IPF maps, a clear black (martensite, M) and white (ferrite, F) lamellar structure is visible, with the width of the lamellae at the sub-micron scale. The selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns for M and F are displayed to the right. Notably, a high density of dislocations is observed in the M region [ 52 ], some of which extend across the interface into adjacent ferrite lamellae. This behavior reduces the dislocation density gradient from martensite to the interface and subsequently into ferrite, thereby mitigating local stress concentrations. Dislocation propagation typically remains confined to a narrow ferrite region adjacent to the interface; therefore, a finer microstructural scale enhances this stress-relief effect.  Fig. 5b  is a TEM image of the impact fracture in longitudinal section at –84 °C. The hard phase M and F undergo coordinated deformation, with no failure voids at the interface, demonstrating that this intense plastic deformation can absorb a large amount of energy [ 53 ]. Interestingly, during plastic deformation, certain martensite lamellae exhibit radial shrinkage, as indicated by the light-colored M lamellae at the bottom of  Fig. 5b . This observation suggests that in sub-micron-scale heterogeneous lamellar dual-phase steel at –84 °C, impact fracture preferentially initiates within the hard martensite phase rather than at the interface or in the soft ferrite phase.

Fig. 5c  presents the high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image of the precipitate phase in HL, with the corresponding SAED pattern of the precipitate displayed on the right. Based on the energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) results shown in  Fig. 5d , the precipitate observed in the HL steel is enriched in Nb and C. Using Gatan DigitalMicrograph software, the interplanar spacing of the precipitate phase was determined to be 0.218 nm, which is consistent with the (200) crystal plane of NbC (theoretical value: 0.223 nm). Considering the HRTEM, SAED, and EDX results comprehensively, the precipitate can be identified as NbC. The precipitate phase exhibits a semi-coherent relationship with the ferrite matrix, which has an interplanar spacing of 0.202 nm. The misfit between the precipitate phase and the matrix can be calculated using the following equation [ 54 , 55 ]:

The calculated misfit degree between the precipitate phase and the surrounding matrix is 7.6 %, indicating a very low misfit. This suggests that NbC serves as a favorable nucleation site for the heterogeneous nucleation of ferrite in the matrix. The introduction of NbC precipitates promotes the nucleation of the matrix, facilitating the refinement of martensite and ferrite lamellae [ 56 ]. To evaluate the size distribution of NbC precipitates in HL, Image-Pro Plus software was used to perform a statistical analysis of precipitate sizes in the experimental steel. Images were randomly selected to calculate the particle size distribution, with the statistical results shown in  Fig. 5e . The results reveal that the average diameter of the precipitates in the experimental steel is 11.9 nm. The strengthening effect of these nanoscale precipitates on HL will be discussed in detail in the following sections.

sections.heading: EDS characterization
paragraphs:
Elemental distribution in HL steel was measured using EDS, as shown in  Fig. 6 
                         .  Fig. 6a  shows the line scan path, and the line profile in  Fig. 6b  corresponds to the line scan results in (a) (For clarity, the elemental signals have been appropriately shifted, so the relative content comparison between elements is not meaningful). The results indicate that Ni and Mn concentrations are significantly higher in the martensite phase than in the ferrite phase, whereas the concentrations of other elements remain largely unchanged between the two microstructures. To quantitatively assess the Mn and Ni content differences between ferrite and martensite, numerous points along the lamellae in the line scan path were selected for point analysis. The statistical results are shown in the bar chart of  Fig. 6b . The average Ni content in the martensite and ferrite of HL is 6.1 wt% and 4.3 wt%, respectively. The average Mn content in the martensite and ferrite of HL is 1.8 wt% and 1.0 wt%, respectively. In MS, where only a single-phase martensite exists, the Ni and Mn content is theoretically between the levels of the two phases. Therefore, compared to the single-phase martensitic steel MS, the martensite in HL contains elevated levels of Ni and Mn. It is noteworthy that the instrumented impact test results indicate that the crack initiation energies of HL and MS are comparable (39 J vs. 42 J), suggesting that the primary crack initiation sites in HL are still located within the martensitic phase. The reduced crack initiation energy of HL is attributed to the increased nanohardness (reduced low-temperature toughness) of the martensitic phase, resulting from elemental segregation of Ni and Mn [ 57 , 58 ].

Furthermore, previous studies have shown that in conventional bulk ferrite-martensite dual-phase steels, the relative Mn concentration gradient (defined as the ratio of the difference in Mn content between martensite and ferrite to the nominal Mn content) is approximately 130 %. In dual-phase steels, a lower gradient corresponds to a smaller hardness mismatch between the soft and hard phases, thereby enhancing their deformation compatibility [ 27 ]. In the heterogeneous lamellar structure of ferrite-martensite dual-phase steel in this study, the relative gradient is 70 %, suggesting stronger coordination of deformation between the soft and hard phases compared to conventional bulk ferrite-martensite dual-phase steels.

sections.heading: Deformation mechanisms of microstructures at –84 °C
paragraphs: To further elucidate the plastic deformation mechanism of the HL heterogeneous lamellar dual-phase microstructure, tensile specimens of HL steel were observed at –84 °C under different strains. The results are shown in  Fig. 7a–c . The results reveal that no voids were formed at the interface between the ferrite and martensite phases. The stability of this interface ensures the effectiveness of other strengthening mechanisms. As shown in  Fig. 7a and b , at a strain of 3 %, voids are observed in both the hard and soft phases rather than being confined to the hard phase alone. This indicates that the sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar structure enhances the mechanical compatibility between the soft and hard phases, alleviates the stress concentration typically observed at interfaces or within individual phases during tensile deformation in conventional dual-phase steels, and promotes coordinated deformation between the two phases.

For clarity, the corresponding schematic diagram is shown in  Fig. 7d 
                         . In the initial stage of strain, only the ferrite phase, as the soft phase, undergoes plastic deformation, while the adjacent martensite lamellae show no significant changes. As strain increases further, martensite also undergoes changes to maintain structural integrity, resulting in a synergistic effect between the phases. As shown in  Fig. 3b , the dual-phase lamellar structure in HL has a random orientation; however, a certain number of lamellae in close proximity are often parallel to each other. For clarity, as shown in  Fig. 7d , the lamellae were categorized into two types based on their orientation. One type is oriented nearly perpendicular to the tensile direction (angle >45°), corresponding to  Fig. 7a  and region dⅡ. The other type is aligned nearly parallel to the strain direction (angle <45°), corresponding to  Fig. 7b  and region dⅢ. Based on the observed experimental phenomena, the concept of the Weak Force Area (WFA) is introduced. Previous research has shown that martensite consists of smaller lamellae bound together [ 59–61 ]. As shown in  Fig. 7d Ⅱ, in martensite lamellae, the WFA primarily exists at the boundaries between finer lamellae and is distributed along the direction of the lamellae. This results in the easier formation of voids in lamellae perpendicular to the strain direction at approximately 3 % strain due to the presence of WFA ( Fig. 7a ).  Fig. 5a  shows that a large number of dislocations, nearly perpendicular to the lamellae, invade the ferrite at the martensite-ferrite interface, creating a WFA in the ferrite similar to that in the martensite. This WFA, which is perpendicular to the strain direction, ultimately leads to tearing and void formation as strain increases ( Figs. 7b, d Ⅲ). This suggests that the reason for the increased similarity in properties between the soft and hard phases after the heterogeneous lamellar structure reaches the sub-micron scale is that the sub-micron scale limitation amplifies the effect of high-density dislocations extending from the martensite into the ferrite. This ultimately facilitates the coordinated interaction between the soft and hard phases.

Intense cooperative deformation occurs between the martensite lamellae and the adjacent ferrite. At a strain of 16 %, the region shown in  Fig. 7d  was observed. The martensite lamellae in this region can also be divided, as described earlier, into two parts: perpendicular (blue dashed box) and parallel (yellow dashed box) to the strain direction. The deformation behavior of the ferrite is similar to that mentioned earlier. A significant difference in the spacing between the lamellae in the two directions reveals that the ferrite undergoes noticeable plastic deformation, elongating along the strain direction. Due to the presence of WFA within the martensite, the martensite lamellae cannot solely rely on widening to cooperate in deformation with the ferrite. The elongation of martensite along its longitudinal axis is not constrained by the WFA, causing the martensite within the yellow dashed box in  Fig. 7c  to appear elongated and thinned. In special regions (such as the blue dashed box in  Fig. 7c ), martensite lamellae perpendicular to the strain direction cooperate with the surrounding ferrite through both elongation and deflection. This ultimately results in elongation in the strain direction, ensuring consistency in the material's deformation process. It is worth noting that observations at 3 % and 16 % strain reveal that cracks only exist within a specific phase in a certain direction of the lamellae (either in the martensite phase or near the martensite side in ferrite), with no cracks observed at the soft-hard phase interface. This demonstrates that the sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar structure maintains interface stability during deformation, with the soft and hard phases cooperating to preserve the material's integrity. This mechanism ensures sustained work hardening during the second stage of deformation in HL.

Additionally, based on maintaining the stability of the heterogeneous lamellar structure, the element segregation-enhanced hard phase work hardening also contributes to the improvement of the tensile properties. It is generally considered that work hardening occurs in three stages: a rapid decrease at the early strain stage, a gradual stage during the mid-strain phase, and a decrease during the later strain phase [ 39 ]. During the mid-strain phase, the deformation of certain hard phases primarily contributes to work hardening. At this stage, martensite in both steels undergoes deformation; however, the higher hardness of martensite in HL results in a more pronounced work hardening effect, which effectively improves elongation, provided that the structural integrity of the heterogeneous lamellae is preserved.

sections.heading: Relationship between microstructure and mechanical properties at –84 °C
paragraphs:
The superior strength and ductility of HL are attributed to its carefully engineered sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar structure, which promotes heterogeneous deformation-induced (HDI) hardening [ 62–65 ]. The strength of this effect can be evaluated through LUR tensile tests [ 66 ]. LUR tensile tests were performed with cyclic loading, unloading, and reloading on the samples. As shown in  Fig. 8a 
                         , during the unloading and subsequent loading stages, the curve does not follow a straight line but instead forms a hysteresis loop as illustrated in  Fig. 8b . In contrast, the MS exhibits almost no hysteresis loop during the LUR tensile test [ 37 ]. This reveals that HDI hardening occurs during the stretching of HL, whereas this effect is absent in MS. During the tensile deformation of HL, the soft phase undergoes plastic deformation first, while the hard phase remains elastic. This results in geometrically necessary dislocations being blocked and accumulated by domain boundaries during stretching, ultimately generating long-range internal stresses in the soft phase. These long-range internal stresses can counteract some of the shear stress, leading to enhanced plasticity in the material, a phenomenon known as HDI [ 66 ]. The resulting formula is calculated as follows [ 67 ]:

                         where σ HDI , σ r , and σ u  represent back stress, reloading yield stress, and unloading yield stress, respectively. For clarity, these values are presented in  Fig. 8b . The results for σ HDI , σ r , and σ u  are shown in  Fig. 8c . In HL steel, the HDI stress increases with strain, demonstrating intense continuous HDI hardening. Therefore, HL steel achieves continuous work hardening behavior through the synergistic effect of the cooperative deformation mechanism and the continuous HDI hardening at the heterogeneous structure (lamellar martensite/ferrite interfaces). The coupling effect of this multi-scale deformation mechanism effectively coordinates the inverted relationship between material strength and plasticity, ultimately resulting in an excellent combination of high strength and high plasticity at –84 °C.

The beneficial effect of HDI stress on the strength and toughness of dual-phase steels has attracted researchers' attention, with some results showing similar strength to HL, as shown in  Fig. 8d  [ 27 , 35 , 68–71 ]. It is important to note that, due to the limited focus on this parameter in low-temperature environments, the comparison is made under harsher testing conditions for HL (–84 °C), where the tensile strength at –84 °C is similar to that at room temperature, but with a reduced elongation. Therefore, comparing the HDI value of HL at –84 °C with existing studies at room temperature is meaningful for reference. Throughout most stages of deformation, HL steel exhibits higher HDI stress. In  Fig. 8d , HDI data from existing studies, except for the red data representing lamellar heterogeneous structures, all correspond to blocky, alternately distributed heterogeneous microstructures. During strain, these heterogeneous structures, due to incompatibilities, cause geometrically necessary dislocations to accumulate at phase boundaries, ultimately leading to HDI hardening [ 66 ]. As plastic deformation continues, blocky martensite struggles to provide effective constraint to blocky ferrite, leading to localized stress concentration at the phase boundaries or within ferrite, thereby reducing the trend of increasing HDI stress. As strain further increases, voids and cracks begin to form in the martensite, causing the blocky heterogeneous structure steel to fracture earlier [ 27 ].

In contrast, in the lamellar heterogeneous structure steel represented by HL in this study, the cooperative deformation between the layers prevents excessive stress concentration. The martensite and ferrite lamellae maintain stable and continuous mutual constraint, allowing the HDI stress to steadily increase. Notably, the width of the heterogeneous structure exerts a significant effect on HDI hardening and the plasticity of the material. For comparison, the study by Niu et al. [ 27 ] will be referred to as LD. The size distributions of ferrite and martensite lamellae in both LD and HL are shown in  Fig. 7e . The results show that the average width of the martensite lamellae in HL (LD) is 0.37 (0.91) μm, and the average width of the ferrite lamellae is 0.39 (1.11) μm. The sub-micron width of lamellae in HL is much smaller than the micron-sized lamellae in LD. Moreover, the fitted curves of martensite and ferrite lamellae distributions in HL exhibit greater overlap than those in LD, indicating a smaller size difference between the two phases in HL. In summary, as the heterogeneous microstructure evolves from bulk-like to micron and eventually sub-micron lamellae, the mutual constraint between ferrite and martensite becomes increasingly stable. As the lamellar width decreases, the influence of dislocation propagation on enhancing the mechanical compatibility within the heterogeneous structure is effectively amplified. Their cooperative deformation effect continually strengthens, reducing the possibility of stress concentration during strain and continuously increasing HDI stress. Therefore, at –84 °C, HL steel exhibits sustained work hardening due to the synergistic deformation of the soft and hard phases and the hetero-deformation induced (HDI) hardening provided by the sub-micron-scale heterogeneous lamellar martensite-ferrite structure, thereby achieving enhanced strength and ductility.

Additionally, the nanometer-sized precipitates also play a significant role in enhancing the mechanical properties of the material. The precipitation strengthening mechanism is based on the interaction between mobile dislocations and nanometer-sized precipitates, leading to the repeated formation of Orowan loops [ 72 ]. sections.heading: Effect of microstructure on impact toughness at –84 °C
paragraphs: To further understand how the microstructural features influence fracture behavior, we analyzed the fracture morphology in conjunction with the load–deformation curves obtained at –84 °C. As shown in  Fig. 2d , the load–deflection curve of the MS sample exhibits a cliff-like drop immediately after reaching the peak load, indicating a brittle fracture with minimal energy absorption during the unstable crack propagation stage. In contrast, the HL steel presents a complete load–deflection curve with a characteristic plateau corresponding to unstable crack growth, suggesting significant energy absorption in this stage. This difference highlights the superior fracture resistance of HL at low temperatures, which is attributed to its carefully engineered sub-micron ferrite/martensite lamellar structure. The fracture surface morphologies of the unstable crack propagation regions for HL and MS are shown in  Fig. 9a and b . The unstable crack propagation region of HL contains numerous ductile dimples, with some regions near these dimples exhibiting plastic deformation [ 76 ]. In contrast, the MS steel displays dominant cleavage facets and lacks a distinguishable stage IV region, implying that almost no energy is absorbed during unstable crack growth—a primary cause of its inferior low-temperature toughness. The images in the upper right corners of  Fig. 9a and b  further illustrate the microstructural differences in the unstable crack propagation regions. In this region, HL requires substantial energy consumption due to unstable crack propagation, resulting in no obvious secondary cracks. Compared to MS, only a large number of uniformly dispersed voids were observed in HL. However, in MS, crack propagation proceeds with much lower energy consumption, leading to the formation of numerous secondary cracks with uneven distribution. These observations directly reflect the critical role of the HL microstructure in improving crack resistance and impact toughness at cryogenic temperatures.

As shown in  Fig. 9c and d , a large number of uniformly distributed voids are generated in HL during impact loading. These voids, located beneath the fracture surface, help alleviate stress concentration and dissipate energy during crack propagation, thereby enhancing toughness [ 77 ]. Notably, the SEM image of the impact fracture surface at −84 °C ( Fig. 9a 
                         ) reveals that most voids are located at concave/convex surfaces, indicating that the main crack is deflected as it propagates through these regions. This crack deflection mechanism contributes to the improved impact toughness of HL at −84 °C. In contrast, as indicated by the red dashed region in  Fig. 3e , MS exhibits highly inhomogeneous internal stress distribution [ 78 ]. The voids are confined to localized stress-concentrated areas, leading to insufficient energy dissipation. As a result, cracks propagate rapidly, eventually resulting in brittle fracture [ 77 ].

In addition, HAGBs play a crucial role in the low-temperature toughness of HL steel at –84 °C.  Fig. 10c and d  show the EBSD image of the HL impact fracture surface. The secondary cracks exhibit  trans -granular fracture, with a large number of LAGBs observed in the crack propagation direction. When the main crack reaches the HAGBs, deflection occurs. The higher the proportion of HAGBs, the greater the likelihood of crack deflection, leading to higher impact energy absorption and improved low-temperature toughness [ 77 ].  Fig. 10a and b 
                          show the significant difference in the probability of main crack deflection between HL and MS due to the variation in the proportion of HAGBs. In HL (number of deflections per unit length: 80/mm), the probability of main crack deflection is much higher than that in MS (number of deflections per unit length: 30/mm). Therefore, the introduction of sub-micron martensite and ferrite laths reduced the effective size of the heterogeneous structure, which not only facilitated the coordinated deformation between different phases but also increased the fraction of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) in the material. These effects enable the HL with a sub-micron ferrite-martensite heterogeneous lamellar structure to achieve a synergistic improvement in both strength and plasticity-toughness at low temperatures.

Notably, compared to traditional dual-phase steel with blocky ferrite, the design of the sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar structure significantly promotes the homogenization of HAGBs, thereby effectively preventing brittle fracture during low-temperature impact in conventional dual-phase steel, which occurs due to the reduced density of HAGBs in the ferrite region. Wang et al. [ 35 ] compared the sizes of the cleavage-like fracture surface and dimples, suggesting that in ferrite (lath)-martensite dual-phase steels with a blocky distribution, martensite exhibits better low-temperature toughness than ferrite at low temperatures. The specimen fractures  trans -granularly along the ferrite phase, with the fracture morphology resembling cleavage planes similar in size to ferrite. Zhao et al. [ 79 ] also support this view, attributing the observed result to the presence of HAGBs at the martensite lath boundaries, whereas such HAGBs are absent within the ferrite phase. Consequently, the density of HAGBs in the ferrite phase is relatively lower, leading to a reduction in low-temperature toughness. It is noteworthy that, although the HL material in this study is also a dual-phase steel, its structure effectively differs from the blocky distribution, exhibiting a sub-micron ferrite-martensite heterogeneous lamellar structure. As shown in  Figs. 4d and 8e , both the width of the ferrite phase and the martensite phase are comparable to the width of the martensite lamellae (D block ). The boundaries of both the ferrite and martensite phases are characterized by HAGBs. The introduction of ferrite does not lead to an uneven distribution of HAGBs, preventing regions of reduced low-temperature toughness in the ferrite phase. The material with a uniform sub-micron heterogeneous structure ensures consistent performance.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
This study employs a quenching-intercritical quenching process to fabricate ferrite-martensite dual-phase steel with a sub-micron heterogeneous lamellar structure. A comprehensive characterization of the microstructure and mechanical properties was performed at −84 °C to evaluate the material's performance under extreme low-temperature conditions. The influence of the sub-micron-scale heterogeneous lamellar structure on the mechanical behavior at −84 °C was systematically analyzed. The key findings are summarized as follows: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            The heat treatment process effectively refined the heterogeneous structure (ferrite: 0.39 µm; martensite: 0.37 µm), which promoted a uniform distribution of HAGBs. The novel HL steel exhibits excellent mechanical properties at –84 °C, with an UTS of approximately 1007 MPa, El of 24 %, and Akv of 187 J. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            The well-designed submicron-scale heterogeneous lamellar structure reduced the property mismatch between ferrite and martensite, which significantly enhanced the cooperative deformation ability between the soft and hard phases. In addition, nanoscale precipitates play a crucial role in improving the performance of the dual-phase steel. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The excellent low-temperature toughness at –84 °C is attributed to the sub-micron ferrite and martensite lamellae of similar size. This promotes an increase in the density and uniform distribution of HAGBs in HL, effectively preventing the brittle fracture issues commonly observed in large ferrite regions in dual-phase steels at low temperatures. Voids at the fracture surface can alleviate stress concentration at the crack tip, promote crack deflection, and increase the energy absorbed during unstable crack propagation. Additionally, intense plastic deformation, especially cooperative deformation between the soft and hard phases, was observed below the fracture surface.
